# Cycle 1: Lightning Talks, Round 1 {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Lightning Talks: The Format

* **Two minutes**, strictly timed. Show your rendered report or one slide.
* Cover four things:
  1. Your **question**, in one sentence.
  2. Your **data**, in one sentence.
  3. **One figure** and what it shows.
  4. **One open problem**: something you are stuck on or still deciding.
* Work in progress is the point: unfinished analyses get the most useful feedback.

---

## Your Job in the Audience

For each talk you log in the worksheet, write down:

* **One strength:** a figure, a question, or a choice that worked.
* **One suggestion or question:** specific enough to act on ("label the y-axis with units," not "make it clearer").
* If you know an answer to the speaker's open problem, find them at the break.

The talk order is announced in class. Half the class presents now, half in Cycle 4.

---

## 👥 Paired Exercise 1: Feedback Log (10 min, after the round)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Task

1. During the talks, log at least **three** talks in the worksheet's `talk_log` tibble: speaker, question, strength, suggestion.
2. With your partner, compare logs: which suggestion came up most often?
3. If you presented, write down the feedback you received and **one change** you will make to your report.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Checklist

* One row per talk.
* Suggestions are actions, not judgments.
* Keep adding rows in Round 2.
:::
:::


# Cycle 2: From Functions to an R Package {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Why Write a Package?

* You already write **functions with input checks** (Week 9 and your project).
* A **package** bundles functions with their **documentation** and **tests**, so you and others can `library()` them in any project.
* `r02pro`, the package behind `gm`, is one: data plus help pages, installed like any other package.
* Three helper packages do most of the work:
  * `usethis`: creates the folders and files.
  * `roxygen2`: turns special comments into help pages.
  * `devtools`: loads, checks, and installs the package while you develop it.

---

## Anatomy of a Package

| File or folder | What it holds |
|:---|:---|
| `DESCRIPTION` | Name, title, version, author, license, packages it depends on. |
| `R/` | Your functions, in `.R` files. |
| `man/` | Help pages, generated by `roxygen2` (never edit by hand). |
| `NAMESPACE` | Which functions users can call, also generated. |
| `tests/testthat/` | Tests that re-check your functions after every change. |

A package is just a folder with this structure.

---

## Step 1: `usethis` Builds the Skeleton

```r
# Run in the RStudio Console: these create folders and open a new RStudio
# project, so they are shown here but not run in the slides
install.packages(c("usethis", "devtools", "roxygen2"))   # once

usethis::create_package("~/Desktop/phtools")   # new package folder, opens it
usethis::use_r("rates")                        # creates R/rates.R
usethis::use_mit_license()                     # adds a license
usethis::use_testthat()                        # sets up tests/testthat/
```

* Every step edits files for you and prints what it did.
* Then write your functions in `R/rates.R`.

---

## Step 2: Document with `roxygen2` Comments

```{r}
#' Rate per 100,000 people
#'
#' @param cases Number of events (non-negative numbers).
#' @param population People at risk (positive numbers, in persons).
#' @return Rates per 100,000 people.
#' @examples
#' rate_per_100k(cases = 250, population = 1.2e6)
#' @export
rate_per_100k <- function(cases, population) {
  if (!is.numeric(cases) || any(cases < 0, na.rm = TRUE))
    stop("`cases` must be non-negative numbers.")
  if (!is.numeric(population) || any(population <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))
    stop("`population` must be positive numbers.")
  cases / population * 1e5
}
```

---

## The Function at Work

```{r}
#| error: true
rate_per_100k(cases = 250, population = 1.2e6)
rate_per_100k(cases = c(10, 40), population = c(5e4, 2e5))
rate_per_100k(cases = 5, population = 0)
```

* Lines starting with `#'` are ordinary comments to R: the function runs as is.
* `roxygen2` reads them to build the help page, `?rate_per_100k`.
* `@export` makes the function visible to users of the package.

---

## Step 3: `devtools` Does the Rest

```r
# Run in the RStudio Console inside the package project (not run in the slides)
devtools::document()   # #' comments -> man/rate_per_100k.Rd and NAMESPACE
devtools::load_all()   # load the package as if installed, to try it
?rate_per_100k         # your own help page
devtools::test()       # run everything in tests/testthat/
devtools::check()      # the full check CRAN runs: docs, examples, tests
devtools::install()    # install it; now library(phtools) works anywhere
```

* Push the folder to GitHub and others install it with `remotes::install_github("your-login/phtools")`.

---

## Tests: Your Checks, Saved

```{r}
stopifnot(
  rate_per_100k(1, 1e5) == 1,                        # a known value
  all.equal(rate_per_100k(250, 1.2e6), 250 / 12),    # a second method
  is.na(rate_per_100k(c(NA, 5), 1e5)[1])             # missing in, missing out
)
```

* Silence means every check passed. In a package the same checks become `testthat` tests, for example `expect_equal(rate_per_100k(1, 1e5), 1)` in `tests/testthat/test-rates.R`.
* `devtools::test()` reruns them after every change, so a fix never silently breaks something else.

---

## 👥 Paired Exercise 2: A Documented Function (10 min)

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Task

1. Write `prop_ci(x, n, conf = 0.95)`: the share `x / n` with a normal-approximation confidence interval.
2. Add input checks: `n` positive, `x` between 0 and `n`, `conf` between 0 and 1.
3. Document it with `#'` comments: title, `@param` for each argument, `@return`, `@examples`.
4. Test it with `stopifnot()` on a known value, and show one input check firing.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Checklist

* Standard error: `sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)`.
* Multiplier: `qnorm(1 - (1 - conf) / 2)`.
* Optional, in the Console: `usethis::create_package()` in a scratch folder.
:::
:::


# Cycle 3: Interactive Dashboards with Shiny {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What Is Shiny?

* A Shiny app is a **web page backed by a live R session**: change an input, R reruns, the page updates.
* Every app has two parts:
  * **`ui`**: what the page shows (inputs such as drop-downs and sliders, plus outputs).
  * **`server`**: the R code that turns inputs into outputs.
* Shiny apps run in RStudio, not inside a static document or these slides: today's app code is **shown**, and you run it yourself.

---

## Step 1: Write the Logic as a Function

```{r}
plot_country <- function(data, country_name, years = c(1950, 2019)) {
  if (!country_name %in% data$country) stop("Unknown country: ", country_name)
  data |>
    filter(country == country_name, between(year, years[1], years[2])) |>
    ggplot(aes(year, life_expectancy)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "steelblue") +
    labs(x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy (years)", title = country_name)
}
```

* The app's work lives in an ordinary, testable function.
* If the function is right outside Shiny, the app only has to call it.

---

## Testing the Function First

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center
plot_country(gm, "India", years = c(1960, 2019))
```

---

## Step 2: The `ui`

```r
# Shown, not run: an app only runs in RStudio
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Life Expectancy Explorer"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("country", "Country",
                  choices = sort(unique(gm$country)), selected = "India"),
      sliderInput("years", "Years", min = 1950, max = 2019,
                  value = c(1960, 2019), sep = "")
    ),
    mainPanel(plotOutput("trend"))
  )
)
```

* Each input has an **ID** (`"country"`, `"years"`); the output has one too (`"trend"`).

---

## Step 3: The `server`, Then Run

```r
# Shown, not run: an app only runs in RStudio
server <- function(input, output) {
  output$trend <- renderPlot({
    plot_country(gm, input$country, input$years)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)   # opens the app; press Stop (or Esc) to end it
```

* `input$country` is whatever the user picked; `output$trend` fills `plotOutput("trend")`.
* **Reactivity:** `renderPlot()` reruns automatically whenever an input it uses changes.
* Save `ui`, `server`, and `shinyApp()` in a file named `app.R`; RStudio shows a **Run App** button.

---

## Sharing a Shiny App

* An app needs a running R session, so a plain web page cannot host it.
* Options: **shinyapps.io** (free tier, one click from RStudio), **Posit Connect** at an organization, or **Shinylive**, which runs the app in the browser.
* Static alternatives from this course: a Quarto report with `DT` tables (Week 12), or a parameterized report per state or country.

---

# Cycle 4: Lightning Talks, Round 2 + AI Corner {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Lightning Talks, Round 2

* Same format: two minutes; question, data, one figure, one open problem.
* Keep logging talks in your worksheet's `talk_log`.
* After the round: one minute with your partner to agree on the **one change** each of you will make before submitting.

## AI Corner: The Dashboard That Lost a Factor of 1,000 {background-color="#8e44ad"}

Asked for "a documented function for my dashboard: total population by continent, in millions," an AI wrote:

```{r}
#' Population by continent
#' @param data gm-style data; `population` is in persons.
#' @param yr Year to summarize.
#' @return One row per continent, population in millions.
continent_pop <- function(data, yr) {
  data |>
    filter(year == yr, !is.na(continent)) |>
    group_by(continent) |>
    summarize(pop_millions = sum(population, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6)
}
```

Documented, tidy, exported to the dashboard. Ship it?

## AI Corner: Auditing the Numbers {background-color="#8e44ad"}

```{r}
continent_pop(gm, 2019)
gm |> filter(country == "China", year == 2019) |> pull(population)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
asia_ai <- continent_pop(gm, 2019) |> filter(continent == "Asia") |> pull(pop_millions)
```

1. Asia: `r round(asia_ai, 1)` "million" people, yet China alone has over a billion. A **known value** exposes a factor of 1,000.
2. `?gm`: population is in **thousands**. The `@param` line states a unit nobody checked.

## AI Corner: The Audited Version {background-color="#8e44ad"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#' Population by continent
#' @param data gm-style data; `population`
#'   is in thousands of people (see ?gm).
#' @param yr Year to summarize.
#' @return One row per continent,
#'   population in millions.
continent_pop <- function(data, yr) {
  data |>
    filter(year == yr, !is.na(continent)) |>
    group_by(continent) |>
    summarize(pop_millions =
      sum(population, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e3)
}
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
continent_pop(gm, 2019)
```

* Units come from `?gm`, then a **known value** (China) confirms them.

::: {.callout-important}
*Documentation the AI writes is a claim, not a fact. Check every unit.*
:::
:::
:::

---

## Finishing the Final Project

* **Fresh-clone test** once more, after your last change.
* Re-render, so `report.html` matches `report.qmd`; then commit and push.
* `README.md`: name, NetID, dataset, a **working** video link, signed integrity statement.
